newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Serb minister hits out at "diplomatic gaffe".
newsitem.headline: Serb minister hits out at "diplomatic gaffe".

text.p: A senior member of Bosnia's fledgling inter-ethnic government criticised an international donor conference on Thursday, saying it had failed to accord the state's new council of ministers due respect.
Spasoje Albijanic, a Serb who serves as communications minister in the Bosnia-Herzegovina cabinet, told a news conference that he was not happy with the way he had been received in Brussels.

"There is some discontent," he said. " I would call it a diplomatic gaffe. None of those present have welcomed the new council of ministers ... donors instead address (Moslem Trade Minister Hasan) Muratovic as if he is the head of government."

The council of ministers, named on January 3, is the first cabinet formed by Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation and the Serb Republic under the terms of a peace treaty brokered by the international community.
The loose government is headed by a rotating three-man presidency made up of a ruler from each of the three ethnic factions, a Moslem, a Croat and a Serb.
"Stop pretending that one part is the villain and the other part is not," said Albijanic. "I hope this approach will end and I will be addressed as one of the council of ministers."

Albijanic's comments came after a World Bank official was asked by journalists if the international community was prepared to help fund reconstruction in the Serb Republic while indicted war criminals were still free there.

Muratovic, identified by European Commission officials earlier as head of the Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation, said all parties would try strictly to abide by the terms of the Dayton peace accord and bring indicted war criminals to justice as soon as possible.

But Albinajic then intervened. "People keep invoking Dayton in order to avoid reality," he said. "Criminals, if they are criminals, should be treated in an adequate way but not with an approach that makes war criminals of people just for their political beliefs. Proper proof is needed first."
Francois Lamoureux, deputy director general of the European Commission and responsible for the European Union's aid programme in former Yugoslavia, played down Albinajic's comments.
"When you look at the situation a few months ago, it pleases us that at least we have partners who are talking, working together," he said.
